title: Feature Flags & Progressive Delivery
summary: Deploying code and releasing a feature don't have to happen at the same moment. Learn how flags decouple the two, how progressive rollouts limit blast radius, and why flag debt is the tax you pay for the flexibility.

slides.markdown:
Without flags, deploy and release are the same event: the moment your code reaches production, every user sees it. That coupling means every release carries full risk, and rolling it back means a redeploy.

A **feature flag** is a runtime switch that lets you ship the code dark — merged, deployed, running — while deciding separately, and later, who actually sees the behavior it guards. That single decoupling is what makes progressive rollouts, instant kill-switches, and testing in production possible.

The cost is real: every flag is a live branch in your code, and a flag left in place after the decision is made is technical debt with a name.

slides.sectionTitle: Deploy and release are two different events
slides.markdown:
**Deploy** = the new code is running in production. **Release** = users can see or trigger the new behavior. Without flags, these collapse into one instant, which forces two bad trade-offs: either you deploy at low-traffic hours to limit blast radius (developers working nights), or you accept that every deploy is instantly a full release to 100% of users.

A flag breaks the coupling. You deploy on your normal schedule, dark code sitting behind `if flag_enabled("new-checkout")`, and the release becomes a config change — flip the flag — that can happen independently, gradually, and be reversed in seconds without touching the deployed artifact at all.

slides.subTitle: They don't all have the same lifetime
slides.markdown:
| Flag type | Purpose | Typical lifetime |
|---|---|---|
| **Release flag** | Hide an incomplete feature until ready | Days–weeks, removed after full rollout |
| **Experiment flag** | Run an A/B test, compare variants | Weeks, removed when the experiment concludes |
| **Ops / kill-switch flag** | Instantly disable a risky path under load or failure | Long-lived, sometimes permanent |
| **Permission flag** | Gate a feature by plan tier or entitlement | Permanent, tied to product logic |

Conflating these is where flag systems get messy: a release flag that quietly becomes a permanent permission flag, or an experiment flag nobody ever concludes, both drift into the flag-debt problem later in this topic. Naming the *type* when you create a flag is what makes its expected lifetime, and thus its cleanup, obvious later.

slides.subTitle: 1% → 10% → 50% → 100%, with gates between
slides.markdown:
Instead of flipping a flag from 0% to 100% at once, a progressive rollout increases exposure in steps, watching health metrics between each one and pausing or reverting the moment something looks wrong.

A typical sequence: 1% of traffic for an hour (catch a catastrophic bug on a tiny population), then 10% for a few hours (catch a subtler regression with enough volume to be statistically meaningful), then 50%, then 100%. Each step is a **decision point**, not a countdown timer — it advances only if error rate, latency, and business metrics stay within bounds.

slides.subTitle: The fastest rollback available
slides.markdown:
A **kill switch** is an ops flag purpose-built to be flipped in an emergency: it disables a specific code path (a new payment provider, a recommendation service, a risky query) without touching the deployed artifact at all.

Compare the two rollback paths when something breaks at 2am: a code rollback means reverting a commit, rebuilding, and redeploying — minutes at best, and it undoes *everything* in that deploy, not just the broken piece. A kill switch is a config flip that takes effect in seconds and disables *only* the path that's failing, leaving the rest of the deploy intact.

The practice worth adopting: **any risky new dependency or code path gets a kill switch by default**, decided at build time, not improvised during the incident.

slides.sectionTitle: Gating a code path with a safe fallback

slides.markdown:
A rollout percentage doesn't have to mean "a random 10% of everyone." Flags support **targeting rules** that pick which users see the new behavior:

- **Internal users first** — employees, then a beta cohort, before any real customer sees it.
- **By region** — roll out to a smaller market first, where a bug affects fewer people and is culturally easier to reason about.
- **By account tier or cohort** — enterprise customers might need a slower, communicated rollout; free-tier users can absorb more risk.
- **By consistent user hash** — the *same* user always lands in the same bucket across sessions, so their experience doesn't flicker between old and new on every page load.

That last point matters more than it sounds: an inconsistent bucketing scheme can put one user in the new checkout flow on one request and the old one on the next, which is confusing at best and broken at worst.

slides.sectionTitle: Test both states, not just the new one
slides.markdown:
A flagged feature effectively doubles your code's live configurations: flag-on and flag-off are both running in production simultaneously, often for weeks. Testing only the flag-on path (because that's "the actual feature") leaves the flag-off path — which real users are still hitting — unverified against every change that landed alongside it.

This gets worse combinatorially: two independent flags mean four live combinations, three flags mean eight. Most teams don't test all combinations exhaustively, which is a reasonable trade-off, but the flag-off path for any *active* flag should stay in the regular test suite for as long as real traffic depends on it.

slides.subTitle: Stale flags outliving their decision
slides.markdown:
A release flag exists to answer one question: "is this feature fully rolled out and safe?" Once the answer is yes and it's been at 100% for a while, the flag has no remaining job — but removing it (deleting the branch, hardcoding the new path, cleaning up the flag-off code) is a separate task nobody's on the hook for.

Left alone, flags accumulate. Each one is a live conditional that every future change has to reason about, a combinatorial state the test suite silently isn't covering, and — worst case — a flag someone flips months later assuming it still does something safe, when the code path it guards has since rotted.

Teams that manage this well treat flag removal as **part of the feature's definition of done**, not an optional follow-up, and some enforce it with a dashboard that flags flags stuck at 100% past some age threshold.

Feature flags and deployment strategies like canary or blue-green both limit blast radius, but at different layers and speeds. A canary deploy controls what **percentage of infrastructure** runs the new artifact; a flag controls what **percentage of users** see the new behavior, on infrastructure that's already 100% deployed.

The practical difference is rollback speed and granularity: reverting a canary means shifting traffic back to the old instances — still a deploy-layer action. Flipping a flag is a config change, instantly reversible, and can target one user cohort while a canary can only target "whichever instances happen to receive that traffic." The two compose well together: canary the *deploy*, flag-gate the *risky feature inside it*, so you have two independent levers if something goes wrong.

slides.sectionTitle: When flags themselves cause the incident
slides.markdown:
A team's flag evaluation service had a brief outage. Every flag check that didn't have an explicit fallback defaulted to **enabled** — because the SDK's default-on-error behavior had never been reviewed — and half a dozen unfinished, unreviewed features went live simultaneously to 100% of users for the six minutes the service was down.

The lesson generalizes: **the flag system is now part of your production dependency graph**, and its failure mode needs the same scrutiny as a database's. Default-safe-on-error isn't optional per flag; it should be the SDK's global default, checked once, rather than something every caller has to remember.

The habit worth taking away: treat every deploy as low-stakes, because the risky decision — who sees the new behavior, and how much of it — happens later, in config, reversibly. That's the whole value of the deploy/release split.

The discipline that keeps it from becoming a mess is symmetric to the value: name each flag's type and expected lifetime up front, keep both states tested while the flag is live, and remove it the moment the rollout decision is made. Rollback & Safe Deploys builds on this with how flags fit into a broader rollback strategy alongside health checks and automated triggers.
